approach: Single-arm, multicenter phase I clinical trial. Patients received bowel preparation, followed by oral administration of capsules containing stool from one of three healthy male donors. Anti-PD1 therapy (nivolumab or pembrolizumab) started at least 7 days post-FMT. Outcomes were assessed using RECIST 1.1 criteria. Survival analysis used Kaplan-Meier methods. Metagenomic sequencing was performed on stool samples to analyze taxonomic composition (MetaPhlAn) and functional gene families (HUMAnN). Post hoc subgroup analyses compared responders vs. non-responders and patients with vs. without FMT-specific toxicity (FT) based on microbial and functional profiles.

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Provides long-term survival data (median OS 52.8 months) for a small cohort of advanced melanoma patients treated with oral FMT plus anti-PD1, demonstrating high safety and promising efficacy signals compared to historical controls.
contribution_and_limits.limits: Small sample size (N=20), single-arm design without a control group, and lack of statistical power for definitive conclusions. Results are hypothesis-generating. Patient selection bias (excluded those appropriate for combination therapy).

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Identifies potential biomarkers for response, linking FMT-specific mild toxicity and long-term survival to specific microbial taxa (e.g., SCFA producers) and functional metabolic pathways (glycan modification, SCFA biosynthesis).
contribution_and_limits.limits: Associations are derived from post hoc analyses. Causality between specific microbes/enzymes and clinical benefit is not established. The 'donor effect' could not be clearly disentangled due to the small cohort and mixed donor usage.

key_findings.finding: Median PFS was 29.6 months; median OS was 52.8 months. ORR was 65% (4 complete responses). Safety profile showed no increase in severe immune-related adverse events (irAEs); only grade 3 toxicities occurred.
R patients had significantly longer mPFS (52.8 vs. 5.2 months, p=0.0016) and longer mOS (52.8 vs. 17.6 months, p=0.0628). R patients sustained donor-derived microbial similarity over time.

key_findings.conditions: Patients with FMT-specific toxicity (FT, N=8) vs. Without FT (NFT, N=12)
key_findings.finding: All 8 FT patients were responders. FT patients had significantly improved mPFS (52.8 vs. 15.9 months, p=0.0364) and trend towards improved mOS (53.9 vs. 24.6 months, p=0.0610). FT was associated with enrichment of SCFA-producing taxa and glycan-modifying enzymes.

LTS were enriched for commensal bacteria (Alistipes, Faecalibacterium) and enzymes involved in amino acid/SCFA biosynthesis. STS were enriched for stress-associated oxidative metabolism pathways and Hungatella hathewayi.

problem_or_question: To evaluate whether modifying the gut microbiome via oral FMT from healthy donors can improve the safety, response rate, and survival outcomes of anti-PD1 therapy in patients with advanced melanoma who are naive to advanced-stage treatment, potentially overcoming primary resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs).
research_scope: Advanced cutaneous melanoma patients (N=20), treatment-naïve for advanced disease, receiving oral fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from healthy donors followed by single-agent anti-PD1 therapy. Multicenter phase I trial conducted in Canada.
work_summary: This study reports the final survival outcomes of the MIMic phase I trial, evaluating the safety and efficacy of combining oral FMT with healthy donor stool and anti-PD1 immunotherapy as first-line treatment for advanced melanoma. The trial enrolled 20 patients who received a single dose of FMT followed by nivolumab or pembrolizumab. The primary endpoint was safety, while secondary endpoints included objective response rate (ORR), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS). The study found that the combination was safe, with an ORR of 65%. Median PFS was 29.6 months and median OS was 52.8 months, figures reported as higher than historical randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and real-world data. Post hoc analyses linked clinical responses to specific microbial engraftment patterns and functional metabolic pathways, suggesting that successful microbiome modulation may enhance ICI efficacy.
